_readme: The single source of truth for every Dockerfile finding ImageShrink reports.
Both the Python backend (server/app/services/rule_engine.py) and the TypeScript
extension (vscode-extension/src/rules) read this file. Detection logic is written twice,
once per language, but the user-facing text lives here exactly once - so a hover in the
editor and a finding on the website can never disagree about what a rule means.
severity        critical | high | medium | low | info. The extension maps this onto a
DiagnosticSeverity; users can override the floor in settings.
sizeImpactMb    Roughly how much larger the image is because of this, in MB. 0 when the
rule costs nothing in size (a security or cache finding).
savingsMb       Estimated saving from applying the fix. 0 when it is not a size rule.
dynamicImpact   true when the real numbers come from base-images.json for the specific
image matched, and these static figures are only a fallback.
autoFixable     true when the engine can produce an exact replacement, which is what
makes the light-bulb Quick Fix appear.
Size figures are estimates for a typical project. They exist to rank findings and give a
sense of scale, and are labelled as estimates everywhere they are shown.

rules.title: Base image is much larger than an equivalent variant
rules.problem: This base image ships a full OS with compilers, headers and docs your application never runs.
rules.explanation: Official language images default to a complete Debian userland. The -slim and -alpine variants contain the same runtime with the build toolchain and documentation removed. For anything that is not compiling at container start, the difference is dead weight in every layer you push, pull and scan.
rules.securityImpact: Every package in the image is attack surface and shows up in CVE scans. A slim base typically removes hundreds of packages you were never using.
rules.performanceImpact: Smaller images pull faster on every deploy and cold start, and push faster from CI.

rules.title: Ubuntu base image where a slimmer Debian would do
rules.problem: ubuntu: carries packages and locale data that debian:bookworm-slim omits.
rules.explanation: Ubuntu and Debian share apt and almost all package names, so the swap is usually mechanical. Debian slim variants strip documentation, manpages and locales, and Debian's security cadence is easier to track for a base you rebuild on a schedule. If the container only runs a compiled binary, a distroless image removes the shell and package manager entirely.
rules.securityImpact: Fewer installed packages means fewer CVEs to triage on every scan.
rules.performanceImpact: Marginally faster pulls; the real win is a shorter dependency list to keep patched.

rules.title: Build tooling ends up in the runtime image
rules.problem: This Dockerfile builds and runs in one stage, so compilers and dev dependencies ship to production.
rules.explanation: A multi-stage build compiles in one stage and copies only the built artefact into a clean final stage. Everything the build needed - compilers, headers, node_modules for devDependencies, package caches - is left behind in a stage that is never pushed. This is usually the single largest size win available, and it costs nothing at runtime.
rules.securityImpact: Compilers and package managers in a production image give an attacker tools to build and run new code inside your container.
rules.performanceImpact: The builder stage stays cached, so incremental builds often get faster rather than slower.

rules.title: Base image tag is not pinned
rules.problem: An unpinned or :latest tag means this Dockerfile builds a different image over time.
rules.explanation: latest is a mutable tag. The image you tested and the image CI builds next month can differ by a major version, and a build that succeeded yesterday can fail today for reasons absent from your diff. Pin at least the major and minor version; pin the digest when you need the build to be genuinely reproducible.
rules.securityImpact: You cannot tell which CVEs are in a build you cannot identify, and a scan result stops meaning anything the moment the tag moves.
rules.performanceImpact: Layer cache misses whenever the upstream tag is republished, silently rebuilding everything downstream.

rules.title: Base image tag floats across releases
rules.problem: Tags like lts, stable or a bare major number move to new releases without warning.
rules.explanation: These are better than latest, but they still change under you - node:lts becomes the next LTS line on its release date. For a service you rebuild automatically, pin the minor version so upgrades are something you choose in a reviewable commit.
rules.securityImpact: A moving tag makes it impossible to correlate a running container with a scan result.
rules.performanceImpact: Unannounced cache invalidation when the tag is republished.

rules.title: npm install where npm ci belongs
rules.problem: npm install can resolve different versions than your lockfile and rewrites it in the image.
rules.explanation: npm ci installs exactly what package-lock.json specifies, fails loudly if the lockfile and manifest disagree, and skips the resolution work install has to do. It is both faster and deterministic, which is what you want in a build. Adding --omit=dev also keeps devDependencies out of the image.
rules.securityImpact: install may silently pull a newer transitive dependency than the one you audited.
rules.performanceImpact: ci skips dependency resolution and is typically 2-3x faster in a cold container.

rules.title: devDependencies installed into the runtime image
rules.problem: This install pulls devDependencies, which production never uses.
rules.explanation: Test runners, bundlers, type definitions and linters routinely outweigh the application itself. Pass --omit=dev in the stage that ships, or install everything in a builder stage and copy only the production node_modules forward.
rules.securityImpact: Development tooling widens the dependency tree a scanner has to clear, usually the noisiest part of a CVE report.
rules.performanceImpact: Fewer packages to download and unpack on every uncached build.

rules.title: yarn install without an immutable lockfile
rules.problem: yarn install may update yarn.lock during the build.
rules.explanation: In a build you want the lockfile treated as an input, not an output. Use --immutable (Yarn 2+) or --frozen-lockfile (Yarn 1) so a mismatch fails the build instead of quietly resolving to different versions. Add --production for the stage that ships.
rules.securityImpact: An unfrozen lockfile can pull a transitive dependency you never audited.
rules.performanceImpact: Deterministic installs cache far more reliably.

rules.title: apt package lists left in the layer
rules.problem: apt-get update writes ~40 MB of package lists that are never removed.
rules.explanation: Deleting the lists in a later RUN does not help: the files are already committed to the earlier layer and both copies ship. The cleanup has to happen in the same RUN as the install, chained with &&.
rules.performanceImpact: Smaller layers push and pull faster.
rules.quickFixTitle: Clean up apt lists in the same layer

rules.title: apt is installing recommended packages
rules.problem: Without --no-install-recommends, apt pulls in optional extras alongside what you asked for.
rules.explanation: Recommended packages are conveniences for interactive systems - documentation, editors, whole toolchains dragged in by a single library. In a container they are unused weight. Add the flag and install anything that turns out to be genuinely required by name.
rules.securityImpact: Each unrequested package is more attack surface and more CVE noise.
rules.performanceImpact: Fewer packages to fetch and unpack.

rules.title: apt-get upgrade makes the build non-deterministic
rules.problem: Upgrading packages during a build means the result depends on when you built it.
rules.explanation: Two builds of the same Dockerfile a week apart produce different images, and the difference is invisible in your diff. Pin a base image that is already patched and rebuild on a schedule instead, so upgrades arrive as a reviewable change of base tag.
rules.securityImpact: Cuts both ways: it does pick up patches, but it also makes the shipped package set unknowable, so a scan result cannot be tied to the image.
rules.performanceImpact: Invalidates the layer cache on every rebuild and adds minutes to the build.

rules.title: apt-get update in its own layer
rules.problem: A cached update layer feeds stale package indexes to a later install.
rules.explanation: This is the classic apt caching bug. Docker reuses the cached update layer while the install layer re-runs, so apt looks for package versions that no longer exist on the mirror and the build fails with a 404. Chaining update and install in one RUN keeps them in lockstep.
rules.performanceImpact: Prevents builds that fail on stale indexes and need a --no-cache rebuild to recover.
rules.quickFixTitle: Chain update and install in one RUN

rules.title: pip wheel cache kept in the image
rules.problem: pip caches every downloaded wheel under ~/.cache/pip and it ships with the image.
rules.explanation: The cache exists to speed up repeat installs on a workstation. A container image installs once, so the cache is pure overhead - frequently tens of megabytes, and much more for large scientific packages.
rules.performanceImpact: Nothing lost: there is no second install to accelerate.

rules.title: apk index cached in the image
rules.problem: apk add without --no-cache leaves the package index in /var/cache/apk.
rules.explanation: --no-cache fetches the index, installs, and discards it within the same command. It replaces the older apk update && ... && rm -rf /var/cache/apk/* idiom and is harder to get wrong.

rules.title: The whole build context is copied into the image
rules.problem: COPY . . brings in everything not excluded by .dockerignore - including .git, node_modules and local env files.
rules.explanation: A repository's .git directory alone is often larger than the application. A local node_modules shadows the one you install in the image and can carry binaries built for the wrong platform. Copy the paths you need explicitly, or keep a .dockerignore that is actually complete.
rules.securityImpact: This is the most common way .env files, private keys and cloud credentials end up inside a published image, where anyone who can pull it can read them.
rules.performanceImpact: Any change to any file invalidates this layer and everything after it, so dependency installs re-run on every edit.

rules.title: No .dockerignore in the project
rules.problem: Without a .dockerignore, the entire directory tree is sent to the daemon as build context.
rules.explanation: Everything in the context is uploaded before the build even starts, and anything a COPY matches ends up in the image. A .dockerignore is the cheapest size fix available and the main defence against copying secrets in by accident.
rules.securityImpact: Keeps .env, .git, key material and cloud credentials out of the image and out of the context entirely.
rules.performanceImpact: A smaller context transfers faster and stops unrelated file changes from busting the layer cache.

rules.title: Source copied before dependencies are installed
rules.problem: Copying source before the dependency install makes every source edit reinstall every dependency.
rules.explanation: Docker invalidates a layer and everything below it when its inputs change. With the source copied first, editing one line re-runs the install. Copy only the manifest and lockfile, install, then copy the source - so the expensive layer is cached until dependencies actually change.
rules.performanceImpact: Usually the difference between a several-minute rebuild and a few seconds. The largest build-time win in most Dockerfiles.
rules.quickFixTitle: Copy the manifest first, then install, then the source

rules.title: Consecutive RUN instructions create avoidable layers
rules.problem: Each RUN commits a layer, and a file written in one and deleted in the next still ships in both.
rules.explanation: Chaining related commands with && keeps intermediate files out of the image entirely. Do not overdo it: commands that change at different rates belong in different layers, because merging them throws away useful caching.
rules.performanceImpact: Fewer layers to push and pull, though over-merging costs cache reuse.

rules.title: ADD used where COPY is meant
rules.problem: ADD silently unpacks local archives and can fetch remote URLs.
rules.explanation: That implicit behaviour surprises readers and occasionally extracts something you meant to copy verbatim. COPY does exactly one thing. Keep ADD for the cases that need it - remote URLs with checksums, or a deliberate tar extraction.
rules.securityImpact: ADD with a URL fetches over the network at build time with no integrity check unless you pass one.

rules.title: Container runs as root
rules.problem: No USER instruction, so the process runs as root inside the container.
rules.explanation: Root in a container is root on the host kernel for anything that escapes namespace isolation, and it lets a compromised process rewrite the whole filesystem. Create an unprivileged user and switch to it after the last step that needs elevated permissions.
rules.securityImpact: Turns a code-execution bug into a much wider compromise, and is the finding most container security policies fail a build on.

rules.title: Possible hardcoded secret
rules.problem: This looks like a credential written directly into the Dockerfile.
rules.explanation: Values in ENV and ARG are baked into image metadata and readable by anyone who can pull the image or run docker history - deleting the line later does not remove it from earlier layers. Pass secrets at runtime, or use BuildKit secret mounts for build-time credentials so they never enter a layer.
rules.securityImpact: A credential in a published image should be treated as leaked and rotated, not just removed.

rules.title: Remote script piped straight into a shell
rules.problem: curl | sh executes whatever the server returns at build time, unverified.
rules.explanation: The build trusts that host completely, on every build, with no record of what ran. Download to a file, verify a checksum or signature, then execute - or install from a package manager that does the verification for you.
rules.securityImpact: A compromised or hijacked upstream host executes arbitrary code inside your build, and nothing in the image records what it was.

rules.title: sudo used inside a container
rules.problem: sudo needs a TTY, behaves unpredictably in builds, and is unnecessary here.
rules.explanation: Build steps already run as root by default, so sudo adds a package and a privilege-escalation path for nothing. Use USER to switch accounts when you need to, and drop sudo from the image.
rules.securityImpact: A sudo binary in the image is a ready-made escalation route for a process you deliberately dropped privileges for.

rules.title: No HEALTHCHECK defined
rules.problem: Without a HEALTHCHECK, an orchestrator cannot tell a wedged container from a working one.
rules.explanation: A process that is running but not serving looks healthy to Docker. A HEALTHCHECK gives it a real signal, so a stuck container gets restarted or pulled out of a load balancer. If you deploy to Kubernetes, its own probes supersede this and the finding can be ignored.
rules.performanceImpact: Lets failed containers be replaced automatically instead of absorbing traffic.
